UNCTION, the a & of anointing or rubbing with oil or other fatty matter.

Unction, in matters of religion, is used for the character conferred on sacred things, by anointing them with oil. Undions v/ere very frequent among the Hebrews. They anointed both their kings and high-prieds at the ceremony of their inauguration. They also anointed the sacred vessels of the tabernacle and temple, to fanttify and conf^crate them to the service of God. The unction of kings is supposed to be a ceremony introduced very late among the Chridian princes. It is said, that noQe of the emperors were ever anointed before Judinian, or Judin. The emperors of Germany took the pra&ice from those of the ead ern empire : king Pepin of France was the first who received the undlion. In the ancient Chridian church, urndion always accompanied the ceremonies of baptism and confirmation. Extreme unction, or the anointing persons in the article of death, was also pratdifed by the ancient Chridians, in compliance with the precept of St James, chap. v. 14. and 15 verses ; and this extreme unction the Romish church has advanced to the dignity of a sacrament. In is adminidred to none but such as are affli&ed with some mortal disease, or are in a decrepit age. It is refused to impenitent persons, as also to criminals. The parts to be ae ointed are the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the mouth, the hands, the feet, and the reins. The laity are anointed in the palms of the hands, but prieds on the back of it ; becau/e the palms of their hands have been already consecrated by ordination. The parts abovementioned are anointed in the form of a cross. The pried begins anointing the fick person’s eyes, faying, “ May God, by his holy anointing, pardon you the fins you have committed by the eyes.” In like manner he proceeds to the other parts, varying the words according to the parts he anoints.

undulation.c:
UNDULATION, in physics, a kind of tremulous motion or vibration observable in a liquid, whereby it alternately rifes and falls like the waves of the Tea.

This undulatory motion, if the liquid be smooth and at reft, is propagated in concentric circles, as most people have observed upon throwing a, stone or other matter upon the surface of a stagnant water, or even upon touching the surface of the water lightly with the linger or the like. The reason of these circular nidulations is, that by touching the surface with your finger, there is produced a depression of the water in the place of contact st. By this depression the subjacent parts are moved successively out of their place, and the other adjacent parts thrust upwards, which lying successively on the defending liquid, follow it ; and thus the parts of the liquid are alternately raised and depressed, and that circularly. When a stone is thrown into the liquid, the reciprocal vi brat sons are more conspicuous

Unduiatory' morion is likewise applied to a motion in the air, whereby its parts are agitated after the like manner as waves in the sea; as is supposed to be the cafe when the firing of a musical instrument is struck. This un dulatory motion of the air, is supposed the matter or cause of found.

UNIVERSITY, a colleiftive term, applied to an assemblage of severai colleges, efiablifhed in a city, wherein are professors in the severai sciences, appointed to teach them to ftudems, and where degrees or certificates of study in the divers faculties are taken up.

In each university four faculties are usually taught, theology, medicine, law, and the arts and sciences.

They are called universities, or universal schools, by reason the four faculties are supposed to take in the whole compass of study.

Universities had their first rife in the Xllth and XHIth centuries. Thc-se of Paris and Bologna pretend to be the first that were set on foot ; but they were on a different footing from the universities among usThe u iverfities of Oxford and Cambridge seem entitled to greatest antiqunyof any in the world ; and Baliol and Merton colleges in Oxford, and St Perer s in Cambridge, all made colleges in the XHIth century, may be said to be the first reg Jar endowments of this kind in Eu ope.

URIM' and thummim, among the ancient Hebrews, a certain oracular manner of confuhing God, which was done by the high priest drt fled in his robes, and having on his pe&oral or breast-plate.

Various have been the sentiments of commentators concerning the urim and thummim. Josephus, and federal others, maintain, that it meant the precious (tones set in the high priest’s breast-plate, which by extraordinary luftre made known the will of God to those who consulted him. Spencer believes that the urim and thummini were two little golden figures (hut up in the pectoral as in a purse, which gave responses with an articulate voice. .In st sort, there are as many opinions concerning the urim and thummim as there are particular authors that wrote about them The safest opinion, according to Broughton, seems to be, that the words urim and thummim lignify some divine virtue and power annexed to the breast-plate of the high priest, .by which an oraculous ant ver was obtained from God when he waconfulted by the high priest; and that this was called urim and thummim to express the clearness and perfe&ion which these oracular anlweqs always carried with them ; for urim signifies light, and thummim perfection ; these answers not being imperfett and ambiguous, hke the heathen oracles, but clear and evident. The use made of the urim and thummim was to consult God m difficult cafes relating to the whole state of Israel ; and sometimes in cafes relating to the king, the sanhedrim, the general of the army, or feme other great personage.

URSUS, in zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of ferae. There are six foreteeth in the upper jaw alternately hallow on the inside, and six in the under jaw', the two lateral ones being la bated ; the dog-teeth ale solitary and conical ; the grinders are five or six; the tongue is (smooth ; the eyes are furnished with a niftita- . ting membrane ; the nose is prominent ; and there is a crooked bone in the penis. There are four species, viz . - 1. The ar<stas, or white bear, with an abrupt tail. He is a native of the northern parts of Europe, and feeds upon berries, infers, and the bodies of dead cattle. He is naturally a lazy animal ; but when enraged, he becomes agile and furious, (landing ere<51 and fighting with his forefeet. When lying, he constantly licks his paws. The female admits the male about the end of October, and (he brings forth in 1 12 days. He never attacks a man, unless he be provoked. 2. The meles, has the tail of an uniform colour; the body is asti-coloured above and black below, with a longitudinal black belt across the eyes and ears. He is likewise a native of Europe, and dwells in woods and the clifts of rocks. He feeds upon eggs, infers, the leaves of the lathynus, In the night he

preys upon rabbits, and seldom appears in the day. He isms himsclf up in a den dug in the rarth during the winter, and sucks a pellicle or bladder situate above the anus. 3. The lator, has an annular tail, and a black belt across the eyes. He is found about the sea shores of America. He feeds upon eggs, fowls, snails, <bc. 4. The lufeus, has a long tail ; and th£ body is iron coloured. He is a native ofHudfon’s bay.
